# Agents at Scale Principles {.unnumbered}

Parts I through V built a bounded agent runtime, established how to measure it, and introduced ways to learn from its trajectories. Learning produces candidates for assessment, not a mandatory prerequisite for scale. Part VI changes the count in two directions. One task may be split across separately managed child trajectories joined by handoffs. Many tasks also run at once on shared models, quotas, and sandboxes, so each competes for capacity. Delegation extends the H·S·A exposures across these boundaries: an unsupported result can become another worker's premise, copied state can become stale, and descendant operations can exceed the intended scope unless the runtime constrains them. The controls already required for one agent must continue to hold when work is distributed, and the additional coordination must earn its cost under the task's requirements.

The two chapters take these questions in order. @Sec-vol3-multi-agent compares delegation with a single-agent runtime given comparable resources, including parallel search and tools. It judges accepted-task rate, makespan, and cost under a declared objective, then develops typed handoffs, bounded returns, concurrent integration, descendant cancellation, and authority control. @Sec-vol3-agent-economics builds the full cost and capacity account for one agent or many, relating caching, reasoning budgets, model routing, and spending reservations to accepted tasks. Five principles govern the part.

::: {#pri-vol3-coordination-tax .callout-principle title="The coordination tax"}

**Invariant**: Delegation adds work for handoffs, context delivery, coordination, and integration. The portion on the critical path reduces any elapsed-time gain from parallel work; aggregate resource use also includes work off that path. Under a fixed-work model, serial dependencies limit speedup, and growing overhead can make additional workers slower. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-multiagent-need.

**Implication**: Identify what separate child trajectories contribute beyond the existing single-agent runtime. Represent their dependencies, carry explicit control fields and bounded evidence across handoffs, and measure whether context or task partitioning justifies the added cost. Natural-language task content does not replace runtime-enforced boundaries.

:::

Whether a fleet earns its tax is settled by measurement against a capable baseline. Evidence-bounded deliberation (principle \ref{pri-vol3-test-time-scaling}) already requires accounting for additional search; delegation adds coordination to that account. Give both designs comparable resource ceilings and report what each actually consumes.

::: {#pri-vol3-tri-axial-evaluation .callout-principle title="Tri-axial multi-agent evaluation frontier"}

**Invariant**: A delegation decision depends on accepted-task rate, elapsed time, and cost per accepted task under a declared objective and constraints. Improving at least one measure without worsening the others is a sufficient comparative gain, not the only useful trade-off. A tighter deadline can justify higher spend when the design still satisfies its acceptance and budget requirements. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-multiagent-evaluation.

**Implication**: Compare against a single-agent runtime with the same available tools, search opportunities, and resource limits. Count failed, discarded, and canceled work, state which requirement motivates a trade-off, and retain uncertainty in the outcome estimates. Equal available budgets do not require equal realized expenditure.

:::

A fleet selected under these constraints must still stay bounded. Delegation does not create authority or replenish a spending allowance.

::: {#pri-vol3-monotonic-delegation .callout-principle title="Monotonic delegation"}

**Invariant**: A child's permitted operations and deadline cannot exceed the delegating grant. Consumable budgets additionally require atomic reservations that account for all concurrent descendants; narrowing each child's ceiling alone does not bound their aggregate spend. Delegating a reusable permission does not by itself revoke the parent's copy. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-multiagent-authority.

**Implication**: Enforce permission scope, current lineage status, and budget admission outside the models. Reserve liability before dispatch, propagate cancellation while tracking acknowledgments, and keep unresolved effects and charges assigned until settlement. A parent stopping does not prove that every child or external operation has stopped.

:::

Bounding what a fleet may spend leaves the question of what its spending buys. The answer is the accepted task, the unit that agent evaluation already counts as success (@sec-vol3-evaluation-contract).

::: {#pri-vol3-trajectory-goodput .callout-principle title="Trajectory goodput and the accepted task"}

**Invariant**: Cost per accepted task charges all initiated work within a declared accounting boundary to the distinct tasks accepted under the same assessment contract. Failed and canceled work remains in the cost account; pending verdicts and unsettled liabilities remain explicit. Goodput per dollar counts those accepted tasks per unit of the same total cost. Neither ratio establishes defect-free behavior or substitutes for the task's other constraints. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-agent-economics-accounting.

**Implication**: Compare complete policies under consistent outcome, cost, deadline, and authority requirements. Include assessment, cleanup, shared capacity, and any human work inside the stated boundary. Measure the bottleneck before choosing model, cache, routing, or execution changes; a higher-cost policy can be justified by a declared deadline or acceptance objective.

:::

The chosen objective determines how to compare cost with other outcomes. Capacity analysis must also account for how work arrives and how long each resource is held.

::: {#pri-vol3-heavy-tailed-scheduling .callout-principle title="Trajectory-lifetime capacity and tail-aware scheduling"}

**Invariant**: Different resources have different holding intervals: a trajectory can retain a sandbox while releasing model-service capacity. Mean concurrency relates a matched population's arrival rate to its mean residence time under stable conditions; it does not establish peak occupancy or deadline feasibility. Variability, dependencies, and admission policy affect waiting and must be measured or modeled under explicit assumptions. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-agent-economics-capacity.

**Implication**: Account separately for residence, service demand, and quota consumption, including failed and pending work. Test burst and completion-time behavior at the intended load rather than inferring tail guarantees from averages or imposing a universal utilization threshold. Scheduling and capacity choices must preserve the task's acceptance, isolation, and spending requirements.

:::

The first three principles decide whether a fleet may run, how it is judged, and how it stays bounded; the last two decide what it costs and how much capacity it needs. With every subsystem built and priced, Part VII runs them together on one trajectory.
